articles.title: Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave lands on TIME100 Next list
articles.summary: Shoko Kawata's maternity leave drew mixed reactions in Japan, a country struggling to lift birth rates.
articles.body:
Shoko Kawata, Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave, has been named one of the 100 most influential rising stars by TIME Magazine.

The recognition comes weeks after the 36-year-old gave birth to her first child on 15 September.

Earlier this year, Kawata, who is mayor of Yawata City in Kyoto prefecture, was plunged into a national debate about whether elected officials should take time off for childbirth.

Her decision to take maternity leave drew a mix of support and backlash across Japan, a country that is struggling to lift birth rates.

Some on social media said having a baby is tough and Kawata is doing her best. Japanese society has failed to design systems with pregnancy in mind, one claimed. Another said Kawata is setting a wonderful example by putting her family first and making it easier for other women to enter politics.

But critics argued that stepping away from public duties is "irresponsible", and that if Kawata wanted to get pregnant "she should have done so before taking office". One said top officials wanting to take extended leave "should resign".

Others insisted salaries should be cut during maternity leave.

In a sit-down interview with the BBC before giving birth, Kawata brushed off the criticisms, proudly declaring she enjoys her job and believes now is the time for her to have a child and start a family.

"If we were to criticise politicians taking maternity leave, it means we are effectively excluding all women in their 20s through 40s - women who are capable of becoming pregnant - from public office," she said.

While Japan provides maternity leave for city workers, there is currently no legal framework for local elected officials. So Kawata worked with her office to create a plan. She transferred her authority to her deputy mayor Shigeto Nose for 16 weeks, while working remotely when she could.

On 15 September, Mayor Kawata announced she gave birth to a baby girl. She posted a photo on X , thanking those who had supported her, and doubled down on her goal to advocate for social issues nationwide.

"As I face the countless challenges that lie ahead and learn what it truly means to be a parent, I want to reflect those experiences in real time into the policies I pursue," she wrote.

"I want to confront the many challenges facing parents and children today from that same perspective, as someone living through them myself, and think about how we can find a way forward together."

articles.title: Michael Jordan sold this Ferrari in 2002; it vanished for 24 years until a partial chassis number in an old forum helped in tracing it
articles.summary: Michael Jordan’s 1997 Ferrari 550 Maranello has resurfaced after spending nearly 24 years out of public view.
articles.body: Michael Jordan’s 1997 Ferrari 550 Maranello has resurfaced after spending nearly 24 years out of public view. Jordan sold the red Ferrari through an Illinois dealership in December 2002, after driving it during the final championship years of his Chicago Bulls career. For years, its whereabouts remained unknown, turning the car into one of the better-known missing celebrity Ferraris. Its trail was eventually picked up through a partial chassis number found on an old online forum, which helped researchers identify the car and trace it to California in 2026.How Michael Jordan’s Ferrari vanished for 24 yearsThe story began on 29 May 1997, when Jordan took delivery of the Ferrari 550 Maranello through Foreign Cars Italia in Greensboro, North Carolina. The JOOPITER account of the car records chassis 108712 as having been delivered to Jordan on that date, with the factory warranty booklet still carrying his signature and Durham, North Carolina address.Just over two weeks later, the Ferrari became part of one of the most recognisable scenes from Jordan’s final championship years. On 13 June 1997, he won his 5th NBA title with the Chicago Bulls. Later that evening, he was photographed leaving the United Center in the Ferrari, with a cigar in one hand and the championship trophy in the car.The Ferrari was finished in Rosso Barchetta with a tan leather interior, chrome wheels and an Illinois registration plate reading MJ 5. According to JOOPITER, Jordan used the car for trips to Bulls home games, practices and public appearances, putting roughly 6,400 miles on it during his ownership.The 550 Maranello had a distinctive connection to JordanThe car was also special because Ferrari had made changes to accommodate Jordan’s 6ft 6in height. JOOPITER says the seating position was modified, with the seat rails adjusted and the padding reduced so that Jordan could move the seat further back.The Ferrari itself was an important model for the Italian manufacturer. As Classic Driver explains, the 550 Maranello represented Ferrari’s return to a front-engined V12 grand tourer after more than two decades of mid-engined flagship models. Its naturally aspirated 5.5-litre V12 produced 485 horsepower and was paired with a six-speed manual gearbox in Jordan’s car. Only 3,083 examples were built, according to Classic Driver.Its connection with Jordan eventually reached beyond cars. AutoGuide reported that Nike designer Tinker Hatfield used the Maranello as a design reference for the Air Jordan XIV. Elements including the quilted leather pattern, side vents, tyre-inspired details and the Jumpman badge placement drew from Ferrari’s styling.Jordan later wore the Air Jordan XIV during Game 6 of the 1998 NBA Finals against Utah. JOOPITER notes that he hit the title-winning shot with 5.2 seconds remaining, securing his 6th championship and his final basket as a Chicago Bull.What happened after Jordan sold the FerrariOn 4 December 2002, Jordan sold the Ferrari through Lake Forest Sportscars in Illinois. That transaction marked the beginning of its long disappearance from public view.For nearly a quarter of a century, there were no confirmed public sightings of chassis 108712. ItalPassion reports that the Ferrari remained absent from the public eye for more than 20 years, while AutoGuide says its disappearance gave the car an almost mythical status among collectors and automotive archivists.An old forum post finally provided the missing clueThe search eventually became a long-running investigation led by John Temerian, co-founder of CURATED. According to JOOPITER, the effort lasted around a decade before a breakthrough came from an unlikely place, an old online forum.A partial chassis number found in the forum allowed researchers to reconstruct the Ferrari’s full vehicle identification number. They then compared that information with Ferrari’s historical dealer records. Those records still connected chassis 108712 with Jordan and the MJ 5 registration plate, providing an important link between the missing car and its former owner. The investigation eventually led CURATED to a long-term owner in California who had kept the car away from public attention.The Ferrari returned to Chicago in 2026Temerian eventually acquired the Ferrari without seeing it in person, according to JOOPITER. On 29 May 2026, exactly 29 years after Jordan originally took delivery, the car returned to Chicago.The rediscovery also clarified the Ferrari’s ownership trail. JOOPITER lists the sequence as Foreign Cars Italia, Jordan, Lake Forest Sportscars, a private California collection from 2002 to 2026, and then CURATED in Chicago.The car subsequently returned to public attention through JOOPITER’s Driven to Greatness sale. AutoGuide reported that the auction marked the first public appearance of chassis 108712 in more than two decades. The Ferrari was offered alongside Jordan’s game-worn jersey from Game 3 of the 1998 NBA Finals.JOOPITER estimated the Ferrari at between $700,000 and $1.3 million for its September 2026 auction. That valuation reflects a car with a documented connection to Jordan, rather than simply another 550 Maranello from the same period.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: San Francisco man who quietly walked his dog in a local park left $3.6 million after his death for park improvements, with his will calling for more benches
articles.summary: William Benjamin “Ben” Bobo was a quiet San Francisco resident who spent years walking his golden retriever, Chad, around Alta Plaza Park near his home.
articles.body: William Benjamin “Ben” Bobo was a quiet San Francisco resident who spent years walking his golden retriever, Chad, around Alta Plaza Park near his home. Few people who saw the pair there could have known that Bobo would eventually leave millions of dollars to the city’s parks. When he died in August 2023 at the age of 87, his estate was valued at about $5 million, largely because of the rise in value of properties he owned. His will directed 80% of the estate to the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department, with his wishes focused particularly on park benches. The resulting bequest was about $3.6 million, far more than the city could reasonably spend on benches alone.Ben Bobo's $3.6 million estate goes to San Francisco parksBobo had lived in San Francisco for decades after moving to the city from the Midwest. He worked in the Design Center and ran a furnishings business, while also owning several properties in the city. According to the Recreation and Park Department, he lived on Clay Street with his partner, Rory, and their golden retriever, Chad.Bobo was known as a private and quiet man. He exercised every day, travelled and regularly visited Alta Plaza Park, including its off-leash dog area. The park, located in the Pacific Heights area, became an important part of his routine and was close to his home.After his death, the value of his estate surprised those involved in administering it. The properties had appreciated substantially over the years, leaving an estate much larger than the amount Bobo's original plans may have anticipated.His will divided the estate among relatives, friends and organisations. Of the major charitable allocations, 80% went to the Recreation and Park Department and 20% to the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. The parks department ultimately received approximately $3.6 million.His unusual request was for more park benchesThe most distinctive part of Bobo's bequest was the specific purpose attached to the money.He wanted the funds used to install new park benches, with plaques commemorating Ben, Rory and Chad. The request reflected his connection to Alta Plaza Park and the time he had spent there with his partner and dog.But there was an immediate practical problem. The $3.6 million bequest was simply too large to spend entirely on benches. The Recreation and Park Department told the estate executor that it could not reasonably install enough benches to use the entire amount for that single purpose.Kim Ridinger, who served as executor of Bobo's estate, said the clause in the will dated back decades, from a time when Bobo's properties were worth considerably less. The growth in San Francisco real estate values meant that the eventual bequest was far larger than Bobo may have anticipated.Rather than abandon the original intention, the city worked with the estate to develop a broader plan that would use the money for benches, park furnishings and improvements while remaining connected to Bobo's wishes.Alta Plaza Park is receiving a major shareAlta Plaza Park is at the centre of the spending plan because of Bobo's connection to the site.The city's approved budget allocates about $1.44 million, or 40% of the bequest, towards implementing parts of the park's existing master plan. The work includes repairs to concrete elements, improvements to pathways and accessibility, and changes to site furniture and signage.The plan specifically calls for replacing 11 existing benches and adding 20 new benches on the park's south and east terraces. The project also includes donor recognition connected to Bobo's gift.Alta Plaza Park itself covers nearly 12 acres and features a broad terraced staircase leading up the steep hillside. From the upper sections, visitors can see across San Francisco and the surrounding area. The park also contains an off-leash dog area, a children's playground, sports courts, picnic facilities and existing viewing benches.Another $720,000 will fund benches and park furnishingsA separate 20%, or approximately $720,000, of Bobo's bequest has been allocated for about 50 new benches and other park furnishings at locations across San Francisco.Each of the relevant sites is expected to carry a plaque recognising Bobo, Rory and Chad, preserving the personal connection behind the gift.The allocation is broader than the initial plan reported when the bequest became public in January 2025. At that stage, the Recreation and Park Commission had proposed spending roughly $700,000 on 81 new benches across the city's parks, including 31 at Alta Plaza Park. The later city-approved budget formalised a slightly different allocation, with about $720,000 designated for approximately 50 new benches and other park furnishings.The remaining money will support other park projectsThe final 40%, approximately $1.44 million, is designated for capital projects and refurbishments across the Recreation and Park Department.The official allocation allows the money to support projects including dog play areas, playgrounds and new parks. The department will also recognise Bobo's bequest on projects receiving the required level of funding.This means Bobo's legacy will extend beyond the benches he specifically mentioned in his will. His gift will contribute to improvements at Alta Plaza Park while also helping other public spaces across San Francisco.City formally approved Bobo's unusual bequestThe Recreation and Park Commission first moved to accept the gift in January 2024 after the department was notified of Bobo's death and his bequest. The probate process followed, with the court considering the proposed allocation of the funds.San Francisco's Board of Supervisors ultimately adopted a resolution in July 2025 authorising the Recreation and Park Department to accept and spend approximately $3.6 million from Bobo's estate. Mayor Daniel Lurie subsequently approved the measure.The official resolution describes the purpose of the gift as providing benches, park furnishings and park improvements at various sites across San Francisco.A quiet life remembered through parksThe unusual nature of Bobo's gift has made his story stand out because there was little indication during his lifetime that he intended to leave such a substantial legacy to the city's parks.He was not a major public philanthropist and did not become known for making large charitable donations while alive. Instead, his connection to the parks was largely personal: he lived nearby, exercised regularly and spent time walking his dog at Alta Plaza Park.Now, the city's parks will carry reminders of Bobo, his partner Rory and Chad through the benches and plaques funded by his estate.A man who quietly walked his dog through a San Francisco park for years ultimately left behind millions of dollars that will help people sit, walk, play and spend time in those same public spaces.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2008, an Oregon lawyer kept his 1894 house from a planned takeover for student towers; the transit agency cancelled its acquisition plan
articles.summary: Randal Acker, a Portland lawyer, successfully prevented TriMet and Portland State University from claiming his historic 1894 house for student dorms, showcasing a significant property rights victory.
articles.body: In February 2008, TriMet told Portland business lawyer Randal Acker that its transit project and Portland State University's dormitory project would go ahead without buying or demolishing his 1894 Queen Anne house near the university. The dispute began after Acker bought the house. A records request, neighborhood support and an editorial page all played a part before the agency that wanted the land stepped back.Acker buys the 1894 house at 525 SW Jackson StreetAcker purchased the house in September 2005 for $380,000 as a place to conduct his law practice, and the 1,600-square-foot property was the subject of TriMet’s acquisition efforts, as reported by Willamette Week. The Oregon State Bar Bulletin described the property as an 1894 Queen Anne-style home that housed Acker’s law practice, where two attorneys worked. According to the reported account, the house was named after his Portuguese water dog, Figo.TriMet and Portland State plan to redevelop Block 158Portland State University held a portion of Block 158 while TriMet held the rest. TriMet would buy the remaining land parcels and PSU would donate its shares under a memorandum of understanding between them, according to Willamette Week. The bulletin reports that TriMet used eminent domain to demolish another four nineteenth-century buildings on the same block. Late in 2006, when the project was underway, the agency informed Acker that there was nothing he could do. Because the house had historical significance, TriMet had to prove that no feasible alternative existed to buying and demolishing it.The agency was operating in a legal climate that changed after the Kelo decision. A 2012 TRB/NCHRP legal research digest, The Ramifications of Post-Kelo Legislation on State Transportation Projects, examines how state legislation passed in response to Kelo has affected the use of eminent domain for economic development, for condemning blighted and nonblighted property, and for restricting transfers of condemned property to private parties. It also examines how states have legislatively redefined "public use."Acker's records request exposes the plan to transfer the land to Portland StateAs a result, Acker asked for TriMet's emails about this project for three years, as the same publication describes. It turned out that the intention was to give the land to the university, which was going to build a large dormitory on the site that included Acker's parcel. Also, he questioned how getting rid of the existing businesses would benefit the public interest.The Oregonian editorial of January 7, 2008On January 7, 2008, The Oregonian published an editorial titled "Leave the House Alone," as the Oregon State Bar Bulletin documented. In February 2008, a month later, TriMet sent Acker's firm a letter stating that its project and the university's project would proceed without buying or demolishing Figo House. Mike Robertson, general superintendent of construction for the joint venture building the Green Line, said he acted as a liaison between TriMet, the city and Acker, and that he and Acker developed a cordial relationship. TriMet spent $2 million to beautify the immediate area around the property, a figure Acker cited. Acker thanked the agency for that, said he appreciated public transportation, and added that he had hoped eminent domain would produce better results in the future.College Station rises around the houseConstruction of the dormitory took place within the surrounding area. Construction of Portland State University's $90 million College Station residence hall began in February 2011, as reported by Oregon Live and cited by the legal blog Inverse Condemnation; Oregon Business reported the same figure. During the groundbreaking held in March, the university representatives and contractors dropped by the Figo House with cookies and hard hats. Bill Bayless, CEO of American Campus Communities of Austin, Texas, said the house's position was typical of Portland. In 2011, Acker attached 400 helium-filled balloons to the Figo House's chimney, drawing a comparison with the house in Pixar's Up, as The Oregonian reported.Oregon voters curb private transfers The conflict also took place amid statewide changes. In November 2006, Oregon voters approved Measure 39, which restricted the use of condemnation for private gain. The Pacific Legal Foundation noted that Measure 39 passed by more than a two-thirds margin. The Oregon Secretary of State's official results for the November 7, 2006 general election show that 881,820 voters, or 67.13 percent, voted in favour of the measure. The above-mentioned study also examines how states have redefined "public use" in legislation. articles.title: Hawaii fenced feral pigs out of a damaged native forest; 16 years later woody plants had multiplied sixfold and young tree ferns were up 51.2%
articles.summary: A comprehensive study of Hawaii's Puʻu O ʻUmi Natural Area Reserve reveals significant recovery of woody plants and tree ferns after feral pigs were fenced out for 16 years, highlighting the complexities of ecosystem restoration.
articles.body: Forests recover slowly, often without obvious signs at first. Signs appear in the seedlings sprouting where the soil was once tilled and in the ferns spreading where no plants grew before. Long-term data are essential for showing whether a forest is recovering. A one-time assessment may point to destruction, but only repeat assessments can tell if the destruction recovers. In Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park on Hawaiʻi Island, researchers assessed the impact of feral pigs by comparing forest sites where fencing kept pigs out with sites where pigs remained. They went back to the exact plots, using the same method of measurement.Why feral pigs harm Hawaiian wet forestsFeral pigs change the vegetation of an area through feeding and trampling, and they may also help other species invade, as the researchers argued in their 2011 Ecological Society of America conference abstract and in the peer-reviewed 2012 Biotropica paper that followed. Hawaiian wet forests are particularly vulnerable to feral pig disturbance because many native species evolved without large mammalian herbivores, leaving ecosystems exposed to a type of disturbance that was not historically present. Fencing out pigs is often considered an important first step in conserving these forests.Five paired sites in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, 1994 to 2010Rebecca Cole, Creighton Litton, Michael Koontz and Rhonda Loh reported their results in Vegetation Recovery 16 Years after Feral Pig Removal from a Wet Hawaiian Forest, published in Biotropica in 2012. The study reports a six-fold increase in woody plants rooted in mineral soil at sites without pigs over 16 years, along with a 51.2% rise in the stem density of young tree ferns. At sites with pigs, herbaceous cover fell by 67.9%. The team recorded the amount of ground cover, herbaceous cover, density of tree ferns, and the density, diversity, and rooting substrate of the woody plants, which was either mineral soil or another plant. The first data were collected in 1994 after fencing and elimination of the pigs and then again in 2010.Ground conditions diverged and strawberry guava gained tooThe ground also had changed its appearance by 2010. As is stated in the study, exposed soil covered 32.0 percent of pig presence locations and just 0.08 percent of locations where pigs were absent. On the other hand, litter covered 53.4 percent of pig presence locations and 88.6 percent of sites where there were no pigs. Release from pigs did not mean recovery of only native species. Density of nonnative woody plants such as strawberry guava (Psidium cattleianum), an invasive shrub, increased fivefold at the pig-free sites over the same period.Hakalau Forest refuge: 16 years of monitoring, 1987 to 2004A second record comes from a different forest and a looser form of management. The USGS lists Effects of ungulate management on vegetation at Hakalau Forest National Wildlife Refuge, Hawai'i Island, by Steven Hess, John Jeffrey, Linda Pratt and Donna Ball, published in 2010 in Pacific Conservation Biology. The researchers observed an increase in cover of native ferns, a decline in bryophytes and exposed soil cover, but no explosive growth in alien grass following the decrease in ungulates, in stark contrast to many Hawaiian forests.Six line-intercept transects were monitored, three in areas that had previously experienced high ungulate activity and three in areas with low ungulate activity. Nine plant-cover classes, including native ferns, native woody plants, alien grasses and soil, were surveyed on four occasions over 16 years, as documented by the U.S. Geological Survey.Native fern cover rises at Hakalau, with some differences left unprovenNative fern cover increased considerably at Hakalau, with bryophyte and exposed soil cover decreasing marginally, according to the USGS report. Native plant cover tended to be higher where grazing pressure had been lower, and alien grass and herb cover tended to be higher where it had been greater. These differences were not statistically significant, so they cannot be presented as confirmed effects.What the results mean for managersTaken together, the studies suggest that reducing or excluding non-native ungulates may help native vegetation recover, although the extent of recovery can vary by ecosystem and may depend on additional restoration measures. The above-mentioned study concluded that control of invasive plants and the introduction of rare native species were needed after pigs were removed.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 1916, a New York widow raising five children refused to sell her Manhattan row house; developers put 14- and 15-storey apartment buildings on both sides, leaving her home standing
articles.summary: In the heart of Manhattan, a determined widow raised her five children and resisted developers' offers, leading to the survival of her family’s five-story row house amidst towering skyscrapers. Uncover the story of Mary Cook and her historic home at 249 West End Avenue, standing as a testament to resilience against urban development.
articles.body: The five-story row house at 249 West End Avenue on Manhattan's Upper West Side stands between two much taller apartment buildings. The Landmarks Preservation Commission's West End-Collegiate Historic District Extension Designation Report, adopted on June 25, 2013, states that Clarence True designed the house at 249 West End Avenue in the Romanesque Revival style in 1892 and 1893, with an American basement plan that lowered the stoop nearly to street level. The report calls it one of the few remaining single-family houses on West End Avenue. The commission's building notes describe it as one of four or five similarly designed houses, while Newyorkitecture counts five. That fit the avenue's first phase. Dolkart's 2009 survey, West End Avenue Survey: A Proposal for Historic District Designation, says the first phase of development, largely from 1885 to 1900, created a street of fine, upper-middle-class, single-family row houses, along with a few larger French flats and several churches and other institutional buildings.The Cook family raised five children in the houseFerdinand Huntting Cook and his wife, Mary Aldrich Cook, bought the house and made it the home of their five children. The location suited their two sons, who attended the nearby Collegiate School, as 6sqft reported. On January 3, 1913, Ferdinand left the house and did not return, and his body was found about a month later in a wooded area in Queens, leaving Mary a widow, as Daytonian in Manhattan recounts.Apartment houses of 12 to 16 stories replaced row housesThe designation report explains that after 1900, rising construction costs made new row houses impractical, and the opening of the IRT subway in 1904 made the Upper West Side more accessible to the city's expanding population. The 1901 Tenement House Act, which also regulated light, ventilation, fireproofing and lot coverage, capped building height at one and a third times the width of the street. The ratio was amended to one and a half times in 1902 and remained in effect until 1929.Before World War I, apartment buildings in the area were 12 to 14 stories high, and after the war they rose to 15 or 16 stories. Developers bought row houses less than 30 years old to assemble sites, and Riverside Drive and West End Avenue were especially vulnerable to the trend. Dolkart's survey counted 218 buildings on West End Avenue as of January 2009, including 112 large apartment buildings and 70 narrow single-family homes, many converted to apartments.Mary Cook declines offers as 255 West End Avenue rises 255 West End Avenue rose on the north side of her house. The designation report dates it to 1916 and credits Schwartz & Gross, listing it among the two earliest Colonial Revival apartment buildings in the extension, and New Yorkitecture gives its height as 14 stories. The commission notes that Mary Cook repeatedly declined offers to sell even as similar houses to the north and south were demolished for apartment buildings.243 West End Avenue rises 15 stories to the south The designation report credits Emery Roth with 243 West End Avenue and dates it to 1925, and Newyorkitecture gives its height as 15 stories. Development on the south side was underway in the early 1920s, as 6sqft reported, so the house waited several years for its next neighbor. Developers hoping to assemble the whole block could do nothing without Mary Cook's agreement.The Continental Club moves in and the district is designatedMary Cook died in 1932, as New Yorkitecture and Daytonian in Manhattan note, and the house changed hands. The designation report says the Continental Club was in the building during the 1930s, possibly into the 1940s, offering lectures, musical performances and other cultural events, and its Uptown Gallery showed works by artists including Adolph Gottlieb and Mark Rothko. The house was later converted to apartments. When the extension was designated in 2013, the district consisted of about 220 buildings between West 70th and 79th Streets, and No. 249 is the last survivor of its row, as Untapped Cities notes.You use AI every day. articles.title: In the 1870s, a San Francisco undertaker refused to sell his small house to a railroad millionaire; instead of taking it, the tycoon built a towering spite fence around it
articles.summary: Explore the intriguing story of an undertaker in 1870s San Francisco who refused a buyout from millionaire Charles Crocker, leading to the construction of a towering spite fence around his property.
articles.body: Some people say no to money. Far fewer say no to a railroad millionaire, and fewer still keep saying it while a wall rises outside their windows. On San Francisco's Nob Hill, an undertaker named Nicholas Yung did exactly that. His small house became the centre of a well-known property dispute after he refused to sell to Charles Crocker, who responded by building a 40-foot fence around three sides of the property, as Arnold Woods recounts in his Western Neighborhoods Project article. Putting the undertaker's stand beside a much more recent one in Seattle shows what changed, what did not, and why the law had so little to say about it.A holdout refuses to sell while neighbors doLinda Holden Givens defines the term in her HistoryLink.org essay Edith Wilson Macefield: A House Is Your Home, describing a holdout as someone who refuses to sell property while everyone around her does. The essay adds that in China such houses are known as dingzihu, or nail houses, because they stay put while developments are built around them.Crocker wanted the whole block and Yung would not sellArnold Woods tells the San Francisco side in The Big 4 on Nob Hill: A Closer Look from the Western Neighborhoods Project. Crocker had his house at 1100 California Street built by the same architectural firm, S. C. Bugbee & Son, that designed Leland Stanford's house. Crocker owned a vast area, but he wanted the whole block, and Yung refused to sell. Crocker therefore built a 40-foot fence around three sides of Yung's property, and a footnote in Woods's article traces the account to a San Francisco Chronicle article dated July 27, 1878. Woods writes that after Yung died in 1880, his heirs later sold the property and the house and fence were torn down. Other accounts say Yung's widow, Rosina, held on until she died in 1902 and that their daughters sold the lot to the Crocker family in 1904.Edith Macefield turned down $1 million in Seattle in 2006Givens's essay connects Macefield to a long-standing tradition in Seattle. Princess Angeline, the daughter of Chief Seattle, lived in a waterfront cabin in Seattle despite an 1865 ordinance calling for the removal of Native Americans from the town. She remained there until her death on May 31, 1896. However, she declined both offers due to several reasons which are clearly stated in the essay.One wall shut a neighbor in and another wall rose around herThe San Francisco and Seattle cases ended in a similar picture of a small house walled in, but the walls began with different intentions. Crocker built his fence to enclose Yung's property on three sides. Givens's essay says mall construction began in spring 2006 and had enclosed Macefield's house by 2007. Moreover, the essay mentions that Barry Martin, who was the project supervisor, had introduced himself to her, assured her of help in case of any problem and gradually became her friend. She died on June 15, 2008, leaving the house and its contents to Barry Martin in her will. In July 2009, Martin sold the home to Greg Pinneo of Reach Returns for $310,000. Bridge Group also decided not to buy the adjacent Mike's Chili Parlor because of possible public disapproval.American courts gave holdouts little protection from wallsA neighbor like Yung had few legal options, and the American Planning Association's August 1958 report, Fences, explains why. At common law, an owner was entitled to make reasonable use of his land, and obstructing a neighbor's light, air, or view was no ground for a lawsuit. The English doctrine of ancient lights did not apply in the United States, a position American courts had taken long before 1958, as in the New York Supreme Court's 1838 decision in Parker v. Foote. Because courts were reluctant to treat spite fences as private nuisances, several states, including Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Vermont, Washington, New York and Kentucky, passed statutes allowing suits over them. In the 1880 Connecticut case Gallagher v. Dodge, the motive test was introduced: a fence or building could be considered spiteful if a person of ordinary judgment viewed it that way. The same report noted that the New York act set a fence height limit of ten feet.Cities that tried to ban such fences through zoning struggled. In the 1956 Ohio case State v. Zumpano, a court struck down a Norton Township zoning provision that prohibited unnecessary structures, including fences, whose apparent purpose was to annoy or damage an adjacent owner, because the provision lacked uniform standards for what was prohibited. The report concludes that a city's only direct control over spite fences is height.Seattle's holdouts left spite mounds and a shack on the waterfrontThe HistoryLink article connects Macefield to a long-standing tradition in Seattle. Princess Angeline, the daughter of Chief Seattle, lived in a waterfront cabin in Seattle despite an 1865 ordinance calling for the removal of Native Americans from the town. She remained there until her death on May 31, 1896, as documented by HistoryLink.org. The article also points out that when Denny Hill was leveled in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, certain buildings remained perched on "spite mounds."The Crocker block became the site of Grace CathedralAfter the 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed the Nob Hill mansions, the Crocker family donated their plot to the Episcopal Diocese, which had lost its Grace Cathedral in the catastrophe as well. The cornerstone of Grace Cathedral was laid on January 24, 1910. Construction of the present cathedral began in the late 1920s and proceeded in stages before the completed building was consecrated on November 20, 1964.You use AI every day. articles.title: Dallas gave developers 10 more months to buy its 72-story Bank of America Plaza and keep $103 million in incentives tied to a $409 million plan adding a hotel, garage, restaurant and observation deck
articles.summary: Downtown Dallas is betting that one of its most recognizable towers can have a second act.
articles.body: Downtown Dallas is betting that one of its most recognizable towers can have a second act. The developers behind a sweeping $409 million redevelopment of Bank of America Plaza have been given another 10 months to complete the purchase of the 72-story skyscraper, keeping more than $100 million in public incentives attached to the ambitious transformation, states a report by CRE Daily.A new deadline for a complex dealAccording to CRE Daily report, the Dallas City Council has extended the purchase deadline to July 30, 2027, giving developers Mike Hoque and Mike Ablon additional time to finalize their acquisition of the tower and complete a development agreement with the city. The pair, operating as 901 Main PAHG Partners LLC, announced plans in 2024 to acquire the property from Metropolis Investment Holdings, a Chicago-based investment firm managing the asset for a German family investment group, adds the report.If we go by the report, the original closing deadline was September 30. The additional time reflects the complexity of a transaction that involves not only purchasing the building but also negotiating the public-private development agreement and the extensive redevelopment planned for the property.A $409 million transformationThe acquisition itself is expected to cost more than $165 million. Once completed, the project would substantially change how the landmark tower is used, explains the online report. Office space would shrink from roughly 1.8 million square feet to 1.5 million square feet, with the remaining space undergoing a full renovation. The redevelopment would also introduce 275 hotel rooms, with the project targeting a four-star-or-better standard.A new glass-and-steel structure would house the hotel's lobby and ballroom, while a 1,115-space parking garage would replace a surface parking lot across the street. A skybridge over Main Street would connect the garage to the tower, confirms the report.At street level, the plans call for additional retail space. Higher up, the 69th floor would become home to a restaurant and observation deck, adding a destination component to one of Dallas' most visible buildings.$103 million in public incentivesThe redevelopment is backed by significant public investment. Dallas City Council approved a $103 million payment from the Downtown Connection Tax Increment Financing district last October. The development team has already spent about $4 million on design work and says it has secured a capital partner and financing for the project, although financial details have not been disclosed. Earlier city documents projected completion as early as September 2032, confirms the report.Downtown Dallas is changingThe redevelopment comes as the city's traditional downtown office market undergoes a broader shift. Bank of America, the tower's longtime anchor tenant, is expected to move to a new Bank of America Tower at Parkside near Klyde Warren Park within the next few years. Other major changes are also reshaping Main Street. Neiman Marcus is preparing to close its century-old store at 1618 Main Street, while AT&T is moving its headquarters to Plano, although its lease at One Whitacre Tower runs through 2031.The road aheadBank of America Plaza is not the only downtown property facing pressure. The financial challenges surrounding older office towers, including 2100 Ross, have underscored the difficulties of repositioning aging commercial real estate. For Hoque and Ablon, the project is also their largest redevelopment undertaking to date. Earlier agreements involving Hoque in Fort Worth and Mansfield were terminated over missed deadlines, according to the Dallas Business Journal.The immediate priority is now completing the city's development agreement and closing the tower purchase before July 30, 2027. If the plan stays on schedule, the transformation could coincide with the redevelopment of the nearby Kay Bailey Hutchison Convention Center, a $3.5 billion-to-$3.8 billion project expected to bring additional activity to the western side of downtown.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and istockReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In the 1970s, Newark Airport buried coal fly ash beneath runways built for jumbo jets; more than 20 years later, FHWA said the pavement was still performing well
articles.summary: Discover how Newark International Airport in the 1970s pioneered the use of coal fly ash in runway construction, leading to long-lasting pavements that continue to perform well over 20 years later.
articles.body: The pavement must withstand repeated loads without failing or deforming when airports construct runways for huge planes. Throughout the 1970s, Newark International Airport in New Jersey hosted one of the biggest US operations using coal fly ash in a stabilised pavement base. The stuff wasn't just thrown underground. To make a cementitious base for flexible pavement, engineers used fly ash, lime, Portland cement, and sand. After 20 years or more, the Federal Highway Administration reported that the stabilised parts were still operating satisfactorily. This project was notable because it showed that a material derived from the burning of coal could be made into a structural layer for a large airport. It also provided an early example of the use of an industrial byproduct in the construction of long-life infrastructure.How the airport used the ashIn the early to mid-1970s, construction began at Newark to build or expand runways, taxiways, and aircraft aprons for the jumbo jet era. Federal Highway Administration research on stabilised fly-ash bases indicates that the system was built as a flexible pavement with a stabilised base underneath. The basis was built in three levels with slightly varying mix compositions. Fly ash was 10 to 12% of the mix, and lime and Portland cement were roughly 3 to 4%. The completed stabilised base was 24 to 36 inches deep and provided a major structural layer beneath the asphalt surface of the runway system.The combination used a reaction between the fly ash and the activating ingredients. The reaction caused a cementitious matrix to form that linked the aggregate together, giving the base properties more akin to a layer of low-strength concrete than loose fill. This type of system is called a pozzolan-stabilized base by the FHWA, which is intended to offer load-bearing support under a flexible pavement.The design must also fulfil the requirements for heavier aircraft. The FHWA record shows one mixture with 4% lime and Portland cement reached ultimate strengths of roughly 2,000 to 2,600 pounds per square inch, suggesting the material was being employed as an engineered pavement component rather than as a simple waste-disposal approach.Extended field testWhat makes the Newark experiment especially interesting is that the material had to show itself throughout years of use, not simply in laboratory tests. The FHWA's later examination indicated that the stabilized-base pavement sections appeared to be functioning satisfactorily after more than 20 years of operation. That finding is part of a longer history of using fly ash in pavement bases. The FHWA said stabilized-base compositions containing fly ash have been utilised in the United States since the 1950s, when the material reacts with lime, Portland cement or other activators to generate a binding matrix.The FDA also warned that the system has a flaw: cracking. Stabilised bases may have shrinkage fractures that will eventually reflect through the asphalt surface and increase maintenance requirements. This scenario means that long-term performance depends not only on the mix strength but also on the design, curing, and placement of the base.FHWA's guidance says that the proper mix depends on the type of fly ash, the type of aggregate, the activator, and the moisture conditions. Thus, the Newark experience was not evidence that any coal ash could be easily replaced in a runway. It demonstrated that a carefully formulated blend could operate under challenging conditions.Importance of the Newark ExperimentCoal fly ash used to be considered primarily as a waste product that needed to be disposed of after coal was burnt. Alternatively, it may be used in stabilised pavement bases, putting part of that material into a regulated engineering use where its chemical qualities can add strength. That idea mattered economically as well. FHWA's study has shown that stabilised fly-ash bases usually have been more economical than other base materials in many places, however actual savings will depend on local resources, mix design and building conditions.The initiative also demonstrated the importance of linking material reuse to engineering and not simply substitution. Fly ash varies by source, and its behaviour depends on chemical composition and the activator used. The FHWA advice treats the material as part of a planned stabilized-base system with mix proportions, curing and strength development all influencing performance. That at Newark was particularly apparent, since the pavement was built to carry jumbo-jet loads. Even more than 20 years later, the government evaluation still said the stabilised pavement was performing satisfactorily.The lesson isn't that fly ash makes better runways automatically. It is that an industrial by-product can be turned into a valuable construction material if its chemistry, proportions and long-term behaviour are known. The runway base at Newark is one of the most obvious historic examples of that method in a major US airport project.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Fuel costs: Diesel prices in NI at highest level since Iran war began
articles.summary: The average price of a litre of diesel hit 193.3p this week, according to NI Consumer Council data.
articles.body:
Diesel prices in Northern Ireland are at their highest level since the Iran conflict began, according to Consumer Council data.

It shows that over the past week the average price of a litre of diesel was 193.3p.

That is below the record average of 197.2p in the summer of 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, however some filling stations have already being charging £2 a litre.

Before the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, a litre of diesel cost about 132p.

The Consumer Council data also suggests average petrol prices in Northern Ireland reached a post-Iran war high of 167.2p a litre over the past week.

That compares with about 124p a litre before the conflict began but well below the peak of almost 190p in the summer of 2022.

Data from the UK's Department for Transport shows that motorists in Northern Ireland are more reliant on diesel than those in other parts of the UK.

The figures suggest that just over half the private cars on Northern Ireland's roads use diesel, compared with a UK average of a third.

Sales of new diesel cars in Northern Ireland have fallen sharply in recent years in line with a trend across the UK.

Diesel prices in the UK hit a record high this week and are hovering at just under 200p a litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.

The conflict in the Middle East has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region - that has caused the price of fuels made from oil to surge.

He is also considering a ban on US exports of the fuel as American drivers also face higher fuel costs.

Such a move could bring prices down significantly in the US.

But experts warn that it would put further pressure on diesel prices in other countries, unless they can access further supplies.

The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels a day.

While UK refineries produce more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel to meet the country's needs.

Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of the imports coming from the US.

articles.title: In 2005 Ohio put ground tire rubber into 1 mile of King Road in Sylvania; 10 years later, the recycled section still matched the control at an 87% rating
articles.summary: Discover how a one-mile stretch of King Road, Sylvania, using ground tire rubber as asphalt, maintained an 87% condition rating after a decade—offering insights into sustainable pavement solutions.
articles.body: On one side of the road, engineers applied a one-inch layer of ground tyre rubber as an asphalt overlay, while on the other side, a polymer-modified asphalt portion served as the control. The design of both blends met the Ohio Department of Transportation's requirements. The tyre rubber part and the control had the same pavement condition rating in every year reported in the study, which was a noteworthy outcome of ten years of monitoring. After four years, the rating reached 87%, and during the ten-year observation period, it barely altered. Rubber-modified asphalt is not always superior, according to the test. It has been shown that recycled tyre rubber can create a pavement section with long-term performance comparable to the conventional control under the conditions on King Road.How King Road became a test sectionThe project uses the existing flexible pavement on King Road, Sylvania. The Ohio field report published through the U.S. Department of Transportation research archive says the new surface was a one-inch overlay applied in 2005 across a one-mile stretch. Different asphalt binders were used in the northbound and southbound lanes. One lane employed a modified binder of tyre rubber, or GTR. The control part used a polymer-modified binder. Both were PG rated 76-22 and were formulated to fulfil Ohio DOT criteria for fine-graded asphalt mixes.The road wasn’t a super-heavy truck route. The analysis revealed that the average daily traffic is roughly 7,120 cars per day, of which about 142 are trucks per day. That is important since pavement performance is highly dependent on traffic, climate and the structure underneath the surface. Researchers then followed the two sections rather than judging them after the first few seasons. Their records covered performance and pavement distress over a full decade, allowing the comparison to show how the rubber-modified mix behaved as cracking and other damage developed.The 87% rating was keptThe most popping number from the project is the 87% pavement condition rating. After four years, the PCR increased to 87% and then remained fairly steady, while the GTR and polymer-modified parts had the same PCR score in all years studied, according to the research. There were no cracks in the pavement. Transverse cracks emerged after around 2 years; non-wheel-track longitudinal cracks after 4 years. The fissures became more severe with time. The fourth year was the moment when crack sealing was required. Still, the two parts moved closer together. The study followed both for 10 years and found them to perform well with no significant difference in the pavement condition assessment.These conclusions are further validated by a separate long-term assessment of many Ohio GTR programs. The King Road project was one of the comparisons with a polymer-modified control, and 10-year field data were part of the study on GTR asphalt performance and life-cycle costs.What the outcome showsRoad authorities can use material from discarded tyres to add tyre rubber to asphalt for building of pavements. Ground rubber can change the properties of the asphalt binder, but the ultimate result relies on the rubber, binder, aggregate, mix design, traffic and climate. King Road is thus a representative field example, not a universal formula. The good 10-year performance in the Ohio research itself may have been due to the increased asphalt content used in the combinations on King Road and the relatively low traffic flow on that road.The finding is nevertheless remarkable because the rubber piece didn’t only survive a few years. Over a decade of service, it remained equivalent to the polymer-modified control while reaching the same 87% PCR level. The comparison is especially important because both sides of the road have similar surroundings and traffic. The use of a control section was employed in an effort to assess if the rubber-modified surface was deviating from normal polymer-modified pavement rather than assessing its condition alone.The Ohio research subsequently incorporated the topic into a larger study of GTR pavement performance. That means the King Road project is a real-world test of recycled material against a conventional option. While the road didn't prove all tire-rubber pavement can last 10 years, it did indicate that in this particular one-mile stretch of Sylvania, the recycled method can hold its own over time.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2007, Ohio volunteers saved a 1913 railcar once used as storage and reopened it as a railroad education centre for school and group visits
articles.summary: Discover how a preserved 1913 Pennsylvania Railroad car in Urbana, Ohio has been transformed from storage into the Marion W. Parks Railroad Educational Center, providing valuable railroad history and education to visitors.
articles.body: A 1913 Pennsylvania Railroad car in Urbana, Ohio, had spent years as a building-supply dealer’s office and storage space, which eventually became a small railroad education center. The car was donated to the Champaign County Preservation Alliance in 1999, moved to a new location with help from local groups and the city, and dedicated in 2007 as the Marion W. Parks Railroad Educational Center.The car was built in 1913 at the Pennsylvania Railroad shops in Altoona, Pennsylvania, as an X23 freight boxcar. The railroad faced a shortage of cabooses during World War II and converted 75 X23 boxcars for that purpose. The modifications included bay windows, round windows, a cooking and heating stove, a bunk, a booth, and storage lockers. The converted cars became known as NX23s and were used by the Pennsylvania Railroad during the 1950s and 1960s, which gave the Urbana car a second life on the railroad before it became a piece of local history.A Pennsylvania Railroad Historical Society record of surviving cabooses lists the Urbana car as PRR 478591, which is a wooden Class NX23 with bay windows. The organization’s inventory identifies only a limited number of surviving examples of the railroad’s former caboose fleet.From railroad equipment to storageThe Pennsylvania Railroad sold two of the cars to a local building-supply dealer on Miami Street in Urbana called Marion W. Parks in the late 1960s. Parks used them as an office and for storage, and the railroad car therefore remained part of the local landscape, but no longer had anything to do with moving trains.Only one car was considered salvageable by the time the Parks family donated them to the Champaign County Preservation Alliance in 1999. The preservation group worked with the Simon Kenton Corridor, Simon Kenton Pathfinders, Champaign County Historical Society and the City of Urbana to move the surviving car to its present location at 644 Miami St. The preservation effort was still underway in 2006, and a newsletter from the Lines West Buckeye Region Chapter of the Pennsylvania Railroad Technical & Historical Society reported that the NX23 was already at the Urbana site, although its original interior had been removed and had not yet been restored.The car got a new purposeThe Champaign County Preservation Alliance dedicated the car as the Marion W. Parks Railroad Educational Center in 2007, and the organization now welcomes classrooms, clubs and senior groups for meetings and tours, which gave the former railroad car an educational use after its working life ended. The educational center sits beside the former Pennsylvania Railroad depot, and keeps the caboose and depot together in the same historic area.The car provides a physical way to understand railroad equipment that would be difficult to understand from a textbook. Its windows, stove, bunk and other features were part of the practical arrangements that turned a freight boxcar into a caboose during the wartime shortage.One of a small number leftThe Pennsylvania Railroad Historical Society’s surviving-caboose inventory identifies the Urbana example as an NX23, while the preservation alliance says only four NX23s remain in the United States. The car preserves a particular type of Pennsylvania Railroad equipment that was first built as a freight car, converted for caboose service, sold into private use and eventually rescued by local preservationists. Today, the Marion W. Parks Railroad Educational Center uses that surviving car for school and group visits, and a vehicle that once followed freight trains now sits beside the old depot, with its history available to visitors rather than hidden away as storage space.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kevin O'Leary backed a proposed 40,000-acre Utah AI data-center district with up to 9 gigawatts of power; months later, the project has been downsized and remains stalled after local backlash
articles.summary: Kevin O’Leary backed a proposed 40,000-acre AI data centre district in Utah, with plans for up to 9 gigawatts of power.
articles.body: Kevin O’Leary backed a proposed 40,000-acre AI data centre district in Utah, with plans for up to 9 gigawatts of power. However, months later, the project has been reduced to about 20,000 acres following local opposition, according to Utah Public Radio. Residents have raised concerns about its environmental impact, water and energy use, and the level of public review before the project moves ahead.The proposed Stratos Project is planned for Box Elder County in northwest Utah. The original site covered 40,000 acres, about half the size of Salt Lake City. The area is dominated by ranching, farming and open space and lies north of the shrinking Great Salt Lake, which is also a sanctuary for migratory birds.The project was backed by O’Leary, who said it could strengthen the local economy and increase US computing and energy capacity. The plan included a 9-gigawatt AI data centre, a natural gas plant to power it and other possible facilities.The proposal faced strong opposition from residents. Hundreds attended a Box Elder County Commission meeting in May, where commissioners unanimously approved the project. Residents raised concerns about the scale of the development, its energy and water use, possible environmental effects and the time available to examine the plans.Project size cut in halfBy June 4, O’Leary had agreed to reduce the proposed campus from 40,000 acres to about 20,000 acres, according to Utah Public Radio.The change followed demands from Utah Senate President J. Stuart Adams, who also chairs the agency backing the project. Adams had called for a 75% reduction in size, environmental protections and greater transparency. Despite the change, O’Leary continued to blame misinformation for some of the opposition to the project.The development was planned in phases over several years. O’Leary said developers hoped to have the first gigawatt of data centre capacity operating within two years. The group had already invested about $20 million and planned to seek commitments from potential data centre tenants before raising more money.O’Leary said the project could eventually cost more than $100 billion. He also said it could support about 10,000 construction jobs and 2,000 permanent positions, while generating tax revenue for the state and county.Residents raise environmental concernsThe original 9-gigawatt facility would use more than twice the energy consumed by Utah in a year, according to CNN. But residents questioned what that level of energy use, along with the project's power plant, could mean for the surrounding area.Water use was another concern. Residents feared that cooling the data centre could put additional pressure on the already shrinking Great Salt Lake.“We keep hearing over and over again that we need to pray for rain,” said Sarah Inskeep-Young, who lives in Salt Lake City and has family in Box Elder County. “And now this is coming. What does that mean to the whole state?” She added as quoted by CNN.In response, developers said they would use technologies to reduce water consumption and improve the facility’s power efficiency. They also said the project would follow federal and state environmental regulations.O’Leary also rejected concerns about the lake's water levels. He called worries about draining the lake “ridiculous” and said, “as a graduate of environmental studies, I know what’s on their mind, what they’re concerned about.”Residents, however, said they wanted independent studies before the project moved ahead.“Let’s do an environmental impact study and let’s publish it transparently. Let’s get some things in writing, and let’s give the community some time to review them and give experts some time to review them,” said Caroline Gleich, an environmental advocate and resident of nearby Park City.Referendum application filedThe Box Elder County Commission said it had reviewed more than 2,500 public comments before approving the project. The meeting drew hundreds of people, including residents seeking more information and others protesting the development.Robert Davies, a Utah State University physics professor who studies environmental change, attended the meeting. He said the “overwhelming sentiment was that we don’t have enough information.”The meeting became heated, with shouting and some profanity. Commissioners later moved to a private room, while people in the audience watched the approval through a livestream.Box Elder County Commissioner Lee Perry said the decision was about property rights. “Our vote today is not a vote or against the data center. Our vote is about personal property rights,” Perry said.A group of Box Elder voters also applied to add a referendum to the November ballot seeking to overturn the county commission’s approval.You use AI every day. articles.title: Olivia Dean accused of copying Bill Withers' Just The Two of Us
articles.summary: The star's record label is sued over similarities between her song I've Seen It and  Withers' classic.
articles.body:
British pop star Olivia Dean has been accused of copying the melody of Bill Withers' soul classic Just The Two of Us in a legal case filed in California.

The complaint centres around Dean's song I've Seen It, taken from her Brit Award-winning 2025 album The Art of Loving.

Just The Two of Us was a hit for Withers in 1981, and the publishers of the late singer's catalogue allege that the two songs "share musical features" that are "so striking" they cannot have arisen by coincidence alone.

The lawsuit names Dean's record label Capitol Records, parent company Universal Music Group and her publishing companies as the defendants. It does not seek damages from the singer herself or her co-writers Bastian Langebæk and Max Wolfgang.

In legal documents seen by the BBC, Mattie Music Group, which looks after Withers' back catalogue, said it hired a musicologist to review the two songs.

He concluded "that the works contain substantial similarities" including the "repeated copying" of the melody from Just The Two of Us, the documents said.

The publishers claim they notified Dean's record label of the potential infringement in August, but the music was not pulled from distribution.

To prove plagiarism, Mattie Music Group would have to prove that Dean and her co-writers had previously heard Withers' original composition.

In the lawsuit, they allege that his song's "extraordinary and sustained" commercial success, including "decades of radio play", would mean the musicians had "reasonable opportunity" to have encountered Just The Two of Us before writing I've Seen It.

The defendants have yet to respond to the lawsuit. The BBC has contacted them, and Dean's representatives, for a comment.

How Grammy winner Olivia Dean became Britain's new global star

I've Seen It is the closing track of Dean's breakthrough album, which was released in September 2025.

A sweet, acoustic ballad, it discusses the various types of love she's encountered in her life - from high school crushes to the love she has for her family and friends.

Speaking to W Magazine last year, she said the song was written after "I'd had a lot of red wine".

"When I heard it back for the first time, I burst into tears. It felt like the loveliest note to end on. Whether it's within your friends, your family, or just the love that exists in the strangers around you, it's there, and it's inside of you, too."

It is has been streamed on Spotify about 246 million times, while Just The Two of Us has racked up 948 million plays.

Withers' track went to number two in the US charts in 1981 and earned him a Grammy for best R&B song. He died in 2020.

Dean picked up best new artist at this year's Grammys, while The Art of Loving reached number three in the US and number one in the UK, and was named album of the year at the Brit Awards.

articles.title: In 2004, Little Barrier Island removed invasive Pacific rats; one year later, Cook's petrel breeding success at its hardest-hit sites jumped from 5% to 53%
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking conservation effort, the removal of invasive Pacific rats from Little Barrier Island has led to a remarkable increase in the breeding success of Cook's petrels, from just 5% to 53%. This article explores the impact of predator control on New Zealand's native seabird populations.
articles.body: On Little Barrier Island, also known as Hauturu, in New Zealand’s Hauraki Gulf, the removal of an introduced predator produced a striking change in the breeding fortunes of a native seabird. Pacific rats, known locally as kiore, had been eating the eggs and chicks of Cook’s petrels, a small burrowing seabird that nests on the island. According to PNAS, the 2004 eradication of Pacific rats was followed by a sharp increase in breeding success at two high-altitude Cook’s petrel sites, from about 5% before the eradication to 53% in 2005. The result provided evidence that rat predation had been an important factor behind the earlier breeding failures.The change was especially notable because another introduced predator had been removed decades earlier. Cats were eradicated from Little Barrier Island in 1980, but their removal allowed Pacific rats to become a more important predator of petrel nests. The later rat eradication therefore allowed researchers to see what happened when the remaining introduced mammalian predator was removed.A predator problem hidden in the island ecosystemCook’s petrel (Pterodroma cookii) uses Little Barrier Island as an important nesting site. Cook’s petrels nest in holes where their eggs and chicks become targets for predation. Introduced Pacific rats that had lived on the island for many years ate all kinds of food, including seabird eggs and chicks. Cats that had been introduced at a later time also attacked Cook’s petrels.Research in PNAS also notes that the cats were eradicated in 1980 after a three-year campaign involving traps, dogs and poison. The outcome for the petrels was not entirely straightforward. In two high-altitude research areas, the rate of breeding declined in the years when there were no other mammals besides the Pacific rats. From 1972 to 1979, when cats and rats coexisted, about 32 per cent of the monitored burrows produced chicks. In 1982-2004, when cats had disappeared but rats persisted, the percentage declined to 9 per cent.This pattern fits what ecologists call "mesopredator release". When a larger predator disappears, a smaller predator that it previously suppressed can have a greater impact. In this case, removing cats appears to have left Pacific rats with less predation pressure, while the rats continued to prey on petrel eggs and chicks.The 2004 rat eradicationThen, in 2004, conservation authorities carried out aerial poisoning of Pacific rats with brodifacoum. Subsequent monitoring revealed that the island was now free of introduced mammals. Cook’s petrel responded quickly. Prior to the rat eradication, nesting success in the highland colonies stood at only 5% on average in 2003 and 2004. The following year, which was the first breeding season without the rats, saw nesting success increase to 53%, and for the period 2005 to 2007, it stood at an average of 59%.The Department of Conservation also reported the dramatic change in the early monitoring results. Its 2005 annual report said that around 70% of monitored Cook’s petrel chicks fledged that season, compared with years when as few as 5% survived. The department attributed the improvement to the kiore eradication, while noting that the island still needed continued monitoring before it could be confirmed rat-free. The change was not identical everywhere on the island. At a lower-altitude study site, breeding success remained broadly similar before and after rat removal. Researchers recorded about 66% success in 2003 and 2004 and about 59% after the eradication. This difference showed that the effect of rats varied according to location rather than producing a uniform island-wide response.A recovery that followed the removal of pressureAccording to Emu, Little Barrier Island had been affected by logging, burning, grazing and introduced mammals, but the removal of cats and rats reduced some of the major pressures on its native wildlife. The findings showed that Cook’s petrels living at high altitudes were especially vulnerable to rat predation because their eggs can be left unprotected while incubating, allowing rats to enter burrows and consume eggs or chicks.Little Barrier Island is currently known as an important refuge for Cook’s petrels. Population estimates for 2007, according to New Zealand Birds Online, state that Little Barrier Island is home to 286,000 breeding pairs of Cook’s petrel, the largest population of the species anywhere. In addition, there are other native species that have benefited from the eradication of introduced mammals on the island. The case of Little Barrier Island shows how removing one invasive species can trigger complex ecological changes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'I was not going to let others die' - pilot of Flydubai flight describes cockpit attack by co-pilot
articles.summary: Capt Smit Machchhar tells Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi he opened the cockpit door to let others in during the attack.
articles.body:
Watch: Flydubai pilot speaks with Indian PM

The Indian pilot of the Flydubai plane who was stabbed by his co-pilot and opened the cockpit door to let others in has said he was determined not to let others die.

Capt Smit Machchhar said he was on the floor and still being attacked when he realised the plane carrying more than 170 passengers was sinking and he had to do something.

"I was lying on the floor injured but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside," he said in a video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

"Others came in and also played a role [in controlling the situation]. I was of course fighting for my own life but at the same time I knew I was not going to let others die," he added.

Flydubai's flight FZ1073, which was bound for Tel Aviv from Dubai early on Wednesday morning, plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey.

It first sent an emergency signal to air traffic controllers before switching to code squawk 7500, which indicates hijacking.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later told the media that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.

After fellow passengers overpowered the attacker, two reserve pilots, who were onboard, safely landed the plane at Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia at 06:58 local time.

Machchhar, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Netanyahu, was taken to hospital in Tabuk before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.

Netanyahu told Fox News the attacker was an Omani national and said investigations suggested he had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination" .

He said that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".

The United Arab Emirates has begun investigating "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose", according to the country's state news agency.

Indian social media has been awash with praise for Machchhar since his identity emerged.

He told Modi he had been flying planes for 17 years and "can tell what is happening to the plane even with my eyes closed".

The prime minister told him that "his courage, patience and quick decision-making saved the lives of so many people" and the whole country was proud of him.

The Indian embassy in the UAE on Thursday said Machchhar was "in good health and recovering well". Ambassador Deepak Mittal said he was "proud of Capt Smit for his bravery" and "very reassured" to meet him.

"I am not looking at this wound like a wound because that would make my recovery even more difficult," Machchhar said.

"I am looking at it as a journey which is slowly going on and will take time but I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again."

articles.title: US sending third carrier, about 10,000 more troops to Middle East as Iran tensions persist: Report
articles.summary: The US is reportedly sending a third aircraft-carrier strike group and additional Marine Corps ships to the Middle East, adding about 9,000 to 10,000
articles.body: The US is reportedly sending a third aircraft-carrier strike group and additional Marine Corps ships to the Middle East, adding about 9,000 to 10,000 troops to the region as tensions with Iran remain high.The ships, fighter jets, Marines and sailors are expected to arrive in the region by the end of November, reported The Wall Street Journal. The deployment comes even as there has been a relative lull in direct fighting between the US and Iran in recent days, with Washington continuing to prepare for the possibility of renewed hostilities.The USS Theodore Roosevelt left its home port in San Diego on Sunday on a scheduled deployment, while the USS Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group departed on Monday. The group comprises three amphibious ships carrying Marines from the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit. The crew of the Theodore Roosevelt is preparing for a longer-than-normal deployment, according to senior Navy officialsThe Roosevelt's arrival would add another carrier strike group to a US naval force that already includes the USS George HW Bush and USS George Washington, which are in the Middle East. If the Washington remains in the region when the Roosevelt arrives, the US would have three carrier strike groups there for the first time since April.The three-carrier presence may not be permanent, however. The George Washington could leave the region and return to its home port in Japan. Ships from the USS Boxer Amphibious Ready Group are also in the Middle East.The additional personnel would join more than 50,000 US troops already stationed across the region, according to one US official cited by the Journal.The buildup comes as President Donald Trump continues to leave open the possibility of resuming strikes on Iran. In a TIME interview published Thursday, Trump said it was “possible” the US could resume bombing Iran after the November midterm elections if there is no deal with Tehran. The Wall Street Journal has separately reported that Trump recently told aides he expects bombing Iran to resume in November.Trump's comments came days after he rejected Iran's latest proposal for a seven-day ceasefire. The proposal called for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the resumption of talks over Iran's nuclear programme in return for the US lifting its blockade of Iranian ports.The Strait of Hormuz remains a key point of tension between Washington and Tehran. About a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through the waterway. The US has maintained about 20 Navy ships in the region in recent months to enforce its blockade and help escort commercial vessels travelling through the strait, according to Navy officials.The Pentagon has also extended deployments of other forces that could be involved in any renewed conflict, including air-defence units designed to counter Iranian missiles and drones and the Army's 82nd Airborne Division. The 82nd can carry out a range of missions, including securing airfields and deploying into hostile territory.The additional deployments will further stretch the US Navy, which has faced supply shortages and near-record deployment levels during the conflict. Iran has also fired ballistic missiles at US warships in recent weeks, according to the Journal.
